newsitem.title: USA: Clinton defends use of rosy budget forecast.
newsitem.headline: Clinton defends use of rosy budget forecast.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Saturday defended budget negotiators for putting together a balanced budget deal with help from a last-minute forecast of $225 billion in additional tax revenues projected over five years.

Clinton said White House and congressional budget negotiators allocated only 11.5 percent of the windfall for spending and left the rest for deficit reduction, as part of the plan unveiled on Frtory is, they looked at this pot of money that appeared before them and said, we're going to leave nearly 90 percent of it there for deficit reduction, and try to balance the budget even quicker," Clinton told reporters.

House Minority Whip David Bonior, a Michigan Democrat, Saturday predicted a majority of Democrats in the House would support the budget deal, while Rep. Susan Molinari of New York forecast the overwhelming support of her fellow Republicans.
Both were interviewed on CNN's "Inside Politics" program.

But some Democrats were skeptical, including Rep. Charlie Rangel of New York who called the budget "a Republican bill" and told CNN's "Evans & Novak" that "the poor and the working poor get absolutely nothing out of the tax benefits."

The negotiators were closing in on a budget deal on Thursday night when the Congressional Budget Office gave them a gift. It said that because of the continued strong economy, it had revised its five-year estimates of projected tax revenues to include an additional $225 billion.

White House officials said the forecast of this sum provided a cushion for negotiators to use in settling some of the most controversial elements of the balanced budget deal. It helped quiet a revolt against the plan by Democrats in the House of Representatives.

Clinton said he wanted to compliment those who worked out the agreement because "they didn't try to spend that money." He said some of the windfall that was allocated for spending was designated for the Defense Department.
"Yes, we took a little of the money," said Clinton. "It gets us a few more votes for the plan."
He said if the projections pan out and the $225 billion actually comes into government coffers, the budget may be in balance even before 2002.

What if the economy does not grow as well as now predicted and the forecasts of tax revenues are wrong? "If they're wrong -- even quite a bit wrong -- this budget will still balance in 2002 because they (negotiators) spent just a little over 10 percent" of the $225 billion, Clinton said.
Sen. Connie Mack, in the Republican radio address, also insisted that negotiators did not rely on rosy scenarios.

"This is not an agreement simply for agreement's sake filled with gimmicks, smokescreens and accounting magic," he said. "It is a real plan for a real balanced budget that controls Washington and places America's interests first."

The deal includes $85 billion in net tax cuts, $34 billion in new spending for the president's priorities, and $115 billion in savings to assure the solvency of the Medicare medical insurance plan for the poor and elderly.
In his radio address, Clinton urged lawmakers to approve the plan when it comes up for a vote in coming months.
"Let us now reach across party lines and seize our chance to balance the budget," he said.

Rep. Bill Paxon of New York, chairman of the House Republican Leadership, speaking on CNN's "Evans & Novak", confirmed that House Speaker Newt Gingrich had told Republican lawmakers not to approve any appropriations bills until Congress has passed the tax cuts included in the budget deal.
"We're going to move very aggressively on the tax cut front," Paxon said.
